title: Faith with reasons, suited to each hearer
source_text: Εἶτά φησιν ὅτι ὁρᾷς ὅπως Πλάτων, καίτοι διαβεβαιωσάμενος ὅτι „ῥητὸν“ οὐκ ἔστιν, ὅμως, ἵνα μὴ εἰς ἀνεξέλεγκτον ἀναχωρεῖν δόξῃ, λογισμὸν ὑπέχει ταύτης τῆς ἀπορίας· εἴη γὰρ ἂν τυχὸν „ῥητὸν“ καὶ τὸ μηδέν. ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ τοῦτο φέρει εἰς κατασκευὴν τοῦ δεῖν μὴ ἁπλῶς πιστεύειν ἀλλὰ λογισμὸν ὑπέχειν τῶν πιστευομένων, χρησόμεθα καὶ ἡμεῖς τοῦ Παύλου λέξει ἐγκαλούσῃ τῷ εἰκῇ πιστεύοντι, ἐν ᾗ φησιν· „ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ εἰκῇ ἐπιστεύσατε.“ τὸ ὅσον δ᾿ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ ἀναγκάζει ἡμᾶς ταυτολογεῖν ταυτολογῶν ὁ Κέλσος, λέγων μετὰ τὰς εἰρημένας ὥσπερ ἀλαζόνων ἀλαζονείας ὅτι ὁ Πλάτων οὐκ ἀλαζονεύεται καὶ ψεύδεται φάσκων αὐτὸς καινόν τι εὑρίσκειν ἢ ἀπ᾿ οὐρανοῦ παρὼν ἀγγέλλειν, ἀλλ᾿ ὁπόθεν ἐστὶ ταῦθ᾿ ὁμολογεῖ. εἴποι ἄν τις οὖν καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα. βουλόμενος ἀπαντᾶν τῷ Κέλσῳ, ὅτι καὶ Πλάτων ἀλαζονεύεται ἐν τῇ τοῦ Διὸς κατὰ τὸν Τίμαιον δημηγορίᾳ λέγων· „θεοὶ θεῶν, ὧν ἐγὼ δημιουργὸς καὶ πατὴρ“, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. ἀλλ᾿ εἰ ἀπολογήσεταί τις περὶ τούτων διὰ τὸν νοῦν τοῦ δημηγοροῦντος παρὰ τῷ Πλάτωνι Διὸς, διὰ τί ὁ ἐξετάζων τὸν νοῦν τῶν λόγων τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τῶν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις τοῦ δημιουργοῦ οὐχὶ καὶ πλεῖόν τι ἐρεῖ παρὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ τοῦ Διὸς δημηγορίαν; τὸ γὰρ χαρακτηρίζον τὴν θεότητα ἡ περὶ μελλόντων ἐστὶν ἀπαγγελία, οὐ κατ᾿ ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν λεγομένων καὶ ταῖς ἐκβάσεσι κρινομένων ὅτι θεῖον πνεῦμα ἦν τὸ ταῦτα ἀπαγγέλλον. οὐ πρὸς πάντα οὖν τὸν προσιόντα φαμὲν ὅτι πρῶτον πίστευσον ὃν εἰσηγοῦμαί σοι τοῦτον εἶναι υἱὸν θεοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τὸ πρέπον αὐτοῦ τῷ ἤθει καὶ τῇ καταστάσει προσάγομεν τὸν λόγον, μαθόντες „εἰδέναι, πῶς δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἑνὶ ἑκάστῳ ἀποκρίνασθαι.“ καὶ εἰσὶν οἷς πλεῖον μὴ δυναμένοις τοῦ προτραπῆναι εἰς τὸ πιστεύειν τοῦτο κηρύττομεν, ἄλλοις δὲ ὅση δύναμις ἀποδεικτικῶς δι᾿ ἐρωτήσεων καὶ ἀποκρίσεων προσερχόμεθα. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ λέγομεν τὸ μετὰ χλεύης ὑπὸ τοῦ Κέλσου εἰρημένον. ὅτι πίστευσον ὃν εἰσηγοῦμαί σοι τοῦτον εἶναι υἱὸν θεοῦ, κἂν ᾖ δεδεμένος ἀτιμότατα ἢ κεκολασμένος αἴσχιστα, κἂν χθὲς καὶ πρώην ἐν τοῖς πάντων ὀφθαλμοῖς ἐπονειδιστότατα κεκαλινδημένος. οὐδέ φαμεν· ταύτῃ καὶ μᾶλλον πίστευσον. εἰς ἕκαστον γὰρ πειρώμεθα λέγειν καὶ πλείονα ὧν ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ἐξεθέμεθα.
pass_a_gloss: Then he says that: you see (ὁράω) how Plato, though having firmly affirmed (διαβεβαιόομαι) that it is not 'sayable (ῥητόν)', nevertheless, so as not to seem to withdraw (ἀναχωρέω) into the unexaminable (ἀνεξέλεγκτον), submits (ὑπέχω) a reckoning (λογισμός) of this difficulty (ἀπορία); for perhaps even nothing (τὸ μηδέν) would be 'sayable'. But since he brings this toward establishing (κατασκευή) that one must not simply (ἁπλῶς) believe but submit a reckoning of things believed, we too will use Paul's phrase charging (ἐγκαλέω) the one believing at random (εἰκῇ), in which he says: 'unless you believed at random (εἰκῇ)'. As far as in him, Celsus repeating (ταυτολογέω) compels us to repeat, saying after the mentioned boastings (ἀλαζονεῖαι) as if of braggarts (ἀλαζόνες) that Plato does not boast (ἀλαζονεύομαι) and lie (ψεύδομαι) claiming himself to find something new or, come from heaven (οὐρανός), to announce (ἀγγέλλω), but confesses (ὁμολογέω) whence these are. One might say to these, wishing to meet (ἀπαντάω) Celsus, that Plato too boasts in Zeus's public speech (δημηγορία) in the Timaeus saying 'gods of gods, of whom I am craftsman (δημιουργός) and father', and what follows. If someone defends (ἀπολογέομαι) these through the mind/meaning (νοῦς) of the speaking Zeus in Plato, why will not the one examining (ἐξετάζω) the meaning of the words of the Son of God or of those of the Creator (δημιουργός) in the prophets say something more than the speech of Zeus in the Timaeus? For what characterizes (χαρακτηρίζω) divinity (θεότης) is the announcement (ἀπαγγελία) about future things, not spoken according to human nature (φύσις) and judged by outcomes (ἐκβάσεις) that a divine spirit (θεῖον πνεῦμα) was what announced them. Not to every one approaching do we say: first believe that whom I introduce (εἰσηγέομαι) to you is Son of God, but to each according to what befits (πρέπον) his character (ἦθος) and condition (κατάστασις) we bring the word, having learned 'to know how we must answer (ἀποκρίνομαι) each one'. And there are those to whom, being unable for more than to be urged to believe, we preach (κηρύσσω) this; to others as far as power (δύναμις) demonstratively (ἀποδεικτικῶς) through questions and answers we approach. But we do not say what was said with mockery (χλεύη) by Celsus: believe that whom I introduce is Son of God, even if bound (δέω) most dishonourably (ἀτιμότατα) or punished (κολάζω) most shamefully (αἴσχιστα), even if yesterday and the day before (χθὲς καὶ πρώην) in the eyes of all most reproachfully (ἐπονειδιστότατα) rolled about (καλινδέομαι). Nor do we say: on this account believe even more. For to each we try to say even more than what we set out above.
pass_b_english: Then he says: “You see how Plato, though he has firmly declared that it cannot be ‘spoken,’ nevertheless, so as not to seem to take refuge in what cannot be examined, gives a reasoned account of this difficulty; for perhaps even ‘nothing’ could be ‘spoken.’” But since he brings this forward to establish that one must not simply believe but must give a reasoned account of what is believed, we too shall use the saying of Paul that rebukes the one who believes rashly, in which he says, “unless you believed rashly” (1 Corinthians 15:2).

As far as it rests with him, Celsus, by repeating himself, forces us to repeat ourselves. After the boasts he has already described, as though they were the boasts of impostors, he says that Plato does not boast and lie by claiming that he himself has discovered something new, or that he has come from heaven to announce it, but admits where these things come from.

Anyone who wished to answer Celsus might say in reply that Plato too boasts, in the speech of Zeus in the Timaeus, where he says, “Gods of gods, whose maker and father I am” (Plato, Timaeus 41a), and the rest. But if someone defends these words by appeal to the meaning of the Zeus who makes the speech in Plato, why should not one who examines the meaning of the words of the Son of God, or of the Creator’s words in the prophets, say something even greater than the speech of Zeus in the Timaeus? For what marks out divinity is the foretelling of things to come, things spoken not by the power of human nature and shown by their outcome to have been announced by a divine Spirit.

So we do not say to everyone who comes to us, “First believe that the one I am introducing to you is the Son of God.” Rather, we bring the word to each person in the way that suits his character and condition, for we have learned “to know how we ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:6). There are some to whom we preach this, since they can do no more than be urged to believe; to others we come, as far as we can, with proof by way of questions and answers.

Nor do we say what Celsus said in mockery: “Believe that the one I am introducing to you is the Son of God, even though he was bound in the most dishonourable way or punished in the most shameful way, even though only yesterday or the day before he was knocked about most disgracefully before the eyes of all.” Nor do we say, “For this reason believe all the more.” For on each of these points we try to say even more than we have set out above.

choices.choice: Celsus’s opening words address the reader directly (‘You see’), so they are set as a quotation, with Plato’s word ‘spoken’ (ῥητόν, Seventh Letter 341c) in inner quotation marks. ‘For perhaps even nothing could be spoken’ (εἴη γὰρ ἂν τυχὸν ῥητὸν καὶ τὸ μηδέν) is obscure and may be corrupt; translated literally and taken as Celsus’s words. εἰκῇ in 1 Corinthians 15:2 is usually rendered ‘in vain’; Origen reads it as ‘without thought’, so it is rendered ‘rashly’ both times to keep his argument. The quotation ‘Gods of gods, whose maker and father I am’ is Plato, Timaeus 41a, where Plato’s speaker is the craftsman god; Origen and Celsus call him Zeus. The edition’s full stop before βουλόμενος is ignored, since the participle belongs with τις. διὰ τὸν νοῦν τοῦ δημηγοροῦντος ... Διός is ‘by appeal to the meaning of the Zeus who makes the speech’ (what Zeus stands for in Plato), parallel to ‘the meaning of the words of the Son of God’. οὐ κατ᾿ ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν λεγομένων is rendered ‘spoken not by the power of human nature’, keeping the negation on the manner of speaking. ‘A divine Spirit’ (θεῖον πνεῦμα) is capitalized because Origen means the Spirit who speaks in the prophets. The mocking formula ‘Believe that the one I am introducing...’ is Celsus’s, as Origen says. κεκαλινδημένος (‘rolled about’) is rendered ‘knocked about’; the whole clause points to the Passion, but no single verse is quoted. εἰς ἕκαστον at the end may mean ‘on each point’ or ‘to each person’; the first is chosen. ‘Questions and answers’ echoes the Plato passage quoted in 6.7.
τὸ ὅσον ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ: 'As far as lies with him' changed to 'As far as it rests with him'
τὸν νοῦν τοῦ δημηγοροῦντος Διός: 'the meaning of Zeus’s speech' corrected to 'the meaning of the Zeus who makes the speech' (νοῦς belongs to Zeus as speaker)
οὐ κατ᾿ ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν: 'not spoken within the reach of human nature' changed to 'spoken not by the power of human nature'
notes updated (νοῦς of Zeus, εἰς ἕκαστον ambiguity)
1 Corinthians 15:2, Colossians 4:6, Timaeus 41a checked against the Greek: correct
